mated at 344.3 kcals/day (US Department of Agriculture, 2021), which represents a decrease of 18.5%. This trend was also re-
ported based on analysis of multiple cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (7 cycles spanning
2003–2004 to 2015–2016) (Marriott et al., 2019). American children and adults have reduced their total sugar intake over
time by 27% and 17%, respectively (Marriott et al., 2019). Reductions in the intake of sugar sweetened beverages (SSBs) over
the study timeframe contributed substantially to this reduction. In addition, the US food supply has reduced the number of avail-
able products that contain added nutritive sweeteners, like sucrose and fructose (Popkin and Hawkes, 2016). Compared to 2000,
when 63% of all food and beverage products sold in the US contained added nutritive sweeteners, by 2013, this was reduced to

body weight in the US, in part due to increased energy from high-quality carbohydrates, polyunsaturated fats, saturated fats, and
plant protein (Shan et al., 2019).
